title: The Tiny Cleaner
pitch: A working vacuum cleaner made mainly from a ballpoint pen, capable of sucking up dust.
clue: The proposed suction comes from a tiny motor turning a fan inside the body.
explanation: Tapala Nadamuni built it using a pen and a tiny motor. Guinness documented it in 2024; the device really picked up dust.
summary: Tapala Nadamuni built a working pen-based vacuum. Guinness documented its dust-picking ability in 2024.

title: The Designer Stick
pitch: A patented dog toy shaped like a branch, designed to float and glow in the dark.
clue: The design addresses toys sinking in water and owners losing sight of them in the dark.
explanation: US6360693B1 describes a branch-shaped toy with floating and glowing versions. The patent documents the design; it does not establish commercial sales.
summary: The patent describes a branch-shaped dog toy with floating and glowing versions. It documents an idea, not sales.

title: The Flavour Spoon
pitch: A spoon that uses a weak electric current to make low-salt food taste saltier.
clue: The pitch changes the eating experience rather than adding seasoning to the bowl.
explanation: Kirin launched the Electric Salt Spoon in 2024. It uses a weak current to enhance salty and umami taste; the effect varies by person and dish.
summary: Kirin launched this electric spoon in 2024. It enhances salty and umami taste; experiences vary by person and dish.

title: The Personal Thermostat
pitch: A wearable device that sits against your upper back and can cool or warm that spot.
clue: It works through a contact plate rather than blowing chilled air around the room.
explanation: Sony’s REON POCKET directly cools or warms the area it touches. It is a local thermal device, not a whole-room air conditioner.
summary: Sony’s REON POCKET cools or warms the area it touches. It does not cool the whole room.

title: The Fridge That Visits
pitch: A refrigerator designed to bring itself to you when you call it.
clue: The proposed appliance maps the room so it can avoid obstacles on the way.
explanation: Panasonic demonstrated an autonomous movable fridge concept at IFA 2017. Its sensors let it navigate to a requested location.
summary: Panasonic demonstrated an autonomous movable fridge at IFA 2017. Sensors helped it navigate around the room.

title: The Metal Bicycle Tyre
pitch: An airless bicycle tyre made with flexible metal that springs back after deformation.
clue: Instead of trapped air, the load is carried by a structure made from a special alloy.
explanation: NASA developed a shape-memory-alloy tyre structure and prototyped it for a bicycle. Its flexibility comes from the metal structure, not pressurised air.
summary: NASA prototyped a bicycle tyre using shape-memory metal. Its structure supports weight without pressurised air.

title: The Alarm That Escapes
pitch: An alarm clock with wheels that rolls away beeping so you have to get out of bed.
clue: The wheels are part of the wake-up routine, not a way to move the clock between rooms.
explanation: Clocky is sold as a wheeled alarm that runs away sounding its alarm. The inconvenient feature is the point: you must get up to catch it.
summary: Clocky really rolls away sounding its alarm. Getting out of bed to catch it is the intended feature.

title: The Wearable Nap
pitch: A padded pillow worn over your head, with openings for breathing and resting your hands.
clue: The design targets short naps at a desk rather than replacing a bed pillow.
explanation: Ostrichpillow’s Original Napping Pillow cushions the head and blocks light. Its unusual shape creates a small personal resting space.
summary: Ostrichpillow sells this head-covering napping pillow. The padding cushions the head and blocks light.

title: The Car That Changes Shade
pitch: A car prototype whose outer surface switches between black and white at the push of a button.
clue: The outer surface uses technology related to electronic paper, rather than a fresh coat of paint.
explanation: BMW showed the iX Flow featuring E Ink in 2022. Electrically controlled pigments changed its appearance; this was a research vehicle.
summary: BMW demonstrated the iX Flow in 2022. Electronic-paper technology changed the research vehicle’s exterior shade.

title: The Singing Sweet
pitch: A lollipop that lets you hear music through vibrations while you enjoy the candy.
clue: The proposed sound path goes through contact with your teeth, rather than earbuds.
explanation: Lollipop Star markets candy with bone-conduction audio. Vibrations carry the sound while you eat; it is not an ordinary loudspeaker in the wrapper.
summary: Lollipop Star sells candy with bone-conduction audio. Contact vibrations deliver the sound while you enjoy the sweet.

title: The Banana Bodyguard
pitch: A rigid, banana-shaped travel case made to protect a single banana in your bag.
clue: The shell is meant to protect the fruit from pressure during a journey.
explanation: SafeBanana sells a protective banana case. Its maker says it fits most bananas: a deliberately specific solution to bruised packed lunches.
summary: SafeBanana sells a rigid banana protector. Its maker says the travel case fits most bananas.

title: The Hands-Free Canopy
pitch: An umbrella design supported by a wearable harness instead of a handle you hold.
clue: The support transfers the canopy’s weight to the wearer, leaving both hands available.
explanation: US8944300B1 documents a wearable umbrella supported on the body. This evidence establishes a patented design, not how well every version works.
summary: The patent documents an umbrella supported on the body. It establishes the design, not proof of commercial success.

title: The Self-Parking Slippers
pitch: Slippers fitted with technology that lets them return to their designated spots at a button press.
clue: The proposed parking happens while nobody is wearing them.
explanation: Nissan demonstrated self-parking slippers at a Japanese inn in 2018. Tables and floor cushions also returned to their places in the demonstration.
summary: Nissan demonstrated self-parking slippers at a Japanese inn in 2018. Unoccupied slippers returned to their designated places.

title: The Room That Rearranges
pitch: Robotic furniture that changes a small room between sleeping, working and social space.
clue: The space changes by moving furniture, not by making the building physically larger.
explanation: MIT’s CityHome work led to transformable robotic furniture. Furniture and partitions move so one area can serve different purposes.
summary: MIT’s CityHome project developed transformable robotic furniture, letting the same room serve different purposes.

title: The Space-Material Jacket
pitch: A jacket insulated with aerogel, a material also used in space applications.
clue: The pitch relies on insulation that slows heat transfer, rather than a battery-powered heater.
explanation: NASA describes aerogel technology being adapted into thinner insulated outerwear. The connection is the material; the jacket is not a spacesuit.
summary: NASA describes aerogel insulation adapted into thin outerwear. The space connection is the material, not a spacesuit.

title: The Soundtrack Fork
pitch: A fork designed to detect noodle slurping and trigger a phone to play sounds over it.
clue: A microphone would detect the sound; a phone app would provide the covering audio.
explanation: Nissin announced Otohiko in 2017 with a microphone and phone app. Sales depended on a preorder target; this source establishes the announced concept.
summary: Nissin announced Otohiko in 2017. The fork triggered covering audio from a phone; sales depended on a preorder target.

title: The Compliment Mug
pitch: A travel mug whose lid unlocks only after you say something nice to it.
clue: The pitch uses a microphone and a small latch, not a temperature sensor.
explanation: We wrote this pitch for the game. The voice-controlled latch sounds plausible, but we are not presenting it as a documented invention.
wonder: Which of these would you actually use—even the made-up one?

title: The Lunch-Break Keyboard
pitch: A keyboard that tips its keys sideways each evening to empty crumbs into a removable tray.
clue: The proposed cleaning cycle would run only when the computer is locked.
explanation: This exact keyboard pitch was written for this game. Plausible moving parts are not evidence that the product exists.
wonder: Which everyday annoyance deserves a surprisingly elaborate solution?

title: The Chapter Bookmark
pitch: A bookmark that releases a different scent at each chapter when it reads a tiny printed code.
clue: The proposed bookmark carries replaceable scent cartridges; the paper itself is unscented.
explanation: We invented this chapter-and-scent pitch. A detailed explanation can make an unverified idea sound like a finished product.
wonder: Would adding another sense make this experience better or more distracting?

title: The Meeting Coaster
pitch: A coaster that raises your mug a little each time a meeting runs five minutes over schedule.
clue: The pitch connects a calendar timer to a small lifting platform under the mug.
explanation: This calendar-connected coaster is our fictional pitch. We are not claiming nobody has ever imagined something similar.
wonder: Which invention here solves the problem, and which just makes it more noticeable?

title: The Library Backpack
pitch: A backpack with a zip that slows itself down when a microphone detects a quiet room.
clue: The proposed zip uses a small brake to resist sudden pulling rather than playing masking noise.
explanation: We wrote this noise-sensitive zip pitch for the game. Its explanation is part of the fiction, not evidence of a tested product.
wonder: When would an automatic feature become an annoyance?

title: The Forecast Hanger
pitch: A wardrobe hanger that pushes one outfit forward each morning based on the weather forecast.
clue: The pitch combines a forecast feed with a motorised clothes rail; it does not inspect your plans.
explanation: This particular outfit-selecting hanger pitch is made up for the game. It borrows familiar ingredients to sound convincing.
wonder: What information would this invention need before you would trust it?

title: The Queue Shoes
pitch: Shoes that gently tap your heels when the person ahead moves, using sensors in the toes.
clue: The proposed sensors measure distance ahead; the shoes do not identify people or read a queue number.
explanation: These queue-monitoring shoes are an authored fictional pitch. A believable use case does not establish a real product.
wonder: Which would you borrow for one day but never buy?

title: The Reading-Time Lamp
pitch: A desk lamp that dims whenever it sees you skip a page, then brightens when you turn back.
clue: The pitch tracks printed page numbers with a camera rather than tracking your eyes.
explanation: We made up this page-policing lamp for the game. Its claimed mechanism is invented too, rather than a report of working hardware.
wonder: Which of these ideas gives the user more control—and which takes it away?
